blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: The coefficient of variation (CV) is the SD expressed as a percentage of the mean: CV = (SD ÷ mean) × 100%. It is a unit-free measure of relative spread.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: An SD makes sense only against the scale of the variable. You cannot say whether height (SD in cm) or weight (SD in kg) is “more variable” by comparing raw SDs. Dividing by the mean removes the units.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
Heights with mean 150 cm and SD 10 cm → CV = 10 ÷ 150 = 6.7%. Weights with mean 40 kg and SD 8 kg → CV = 8 ÷ 40 = 20%. Weight’s raw SD is smaller, yet weight is proportionally three times as variable.

Today’s 30 children: CV = 1.75 ÷ 11.81 × 100 = 14.8%.

points.html: CV = (SD ÷ mean) × 100%. Unit-free, so it compares variability across different variables, units or studies.

Meaningful only for ratio-scale data with a positive mean. It fails for interval data such as temperature in °C, where the mean depends on an arbitrary zero, and it becomes unstable when the mean is near zero.
In the laboratory, the CV of repeated measurements of one sample is used to judge an assay’s precision (Reed et al., 2002).
